status: Starting knowledge file. Every technique has verified_by_ravi = false. NIRA must show unverified rules with a visible 'not floor-verified' label. Always follow the ink or chemical maker's technical data sheet.

confidence_key.sourced_multi: Two or more independent public sources agree.
confidence_key.sourced_single: One public source (supplier data sheet, trade guide or patent).
confidence_key.article_only: Taken only from the Textile Learner articles supplied by the user; not cross-checked on the web.
confidence_key.conflict: Sources disagree. Both values are kept in the note. Do not use for decisions until verified.
confidence_key.assumption: No reliable source found. Placeholder only.

artwork_fit_key.SOLID_ONLY: Needs solid single-colour shapes with clear edges. Not for gradients or photo artwork.
artwork_fit_key.SOLID_PREFERRED: Best on solid shapes; fine detail and tone are lost.
artwork_fit_key.TONAL_OK: Can reproduce gradients and photo artwork with halftones.
artwork_fit_key.ANY: Reproduces any artwork including photos, with no screen per colour.

corrections_to_source_articles.article_statement: Described as a form of dye-sublimation that transfers dye onto polyester.
corrections_to_source_articles.correct: Discharge printing removes (bleaches) the existing dye from a dyed ground, mainly reactive-dyed cotton, and can leave a new colour in its place. It does not work on polyester.

corrections_to_source_articles.article_statement: One list names NaCl / Na2SO4 as the acid liberating salt.
corrections_to_source_articles.correct: The burn-out agent is sodium hydrogen sulphate (sodium bisulfate) or aluminium sulphate, which form acid on dry heat and destroy the cellulose. The article's own body text also says this.

corrections_to_source_articles.topic: Thermofixation time for disperse prints on polyester
corrections_to_source_articles.article_statement: Given as 120-130 seconds in one table and 30-60 seconds in the procedure.
corrections_to_source_articles.correct: Not resolved. Stored as 30-130 seconds with confidence 'conflict'.

techniques.name: Plastisol print
techniques.what_it_is: PVC-based ink that sits on the fabric surface and is cured by heat. Opaque, good on dark garments, slightly raised plastic feel.
cautions_fibres: polyester: use low-cure / low-bleed ink because of dye migration

cure_temp_c.published: 320 F through the whole ink film

mesh_tpi.note: See print_rules.json for the full mesh table

risks: Cracking if under-cured or on high-stretch fabric
Heavy hand feel on large solid areas

techniques.name: Water-based pigment print
techniques.what_it_is: Pigment held on the fibre by a binder film. Soft, breathable feel. No washing-off needed.
cautions_fibres: dark garments: weak coverage without a white base or discharge

cure_temp_c.note: Article: polymerise at 135-150 C for 3-5 min. Web sources for water-based garment inks: 149-160 C (300-320 F).

paste_recipe_per_100g.note: Laboratory example from the article for P/C fabric. Factory recipes will differ.

risks: Stiff handle and lower rub fastness with heavy dark shades
Abrasion marks at creases on polyester/cotton
techniques.source: User article 'Pigment Printing on P/C Blended Fabric' ; https://www.learnhowtoscreenprint.com/blogs/news/the-definitive-guide-to-curing-ink

techniques.name: Discharge print
techniques.what_it_is: Water-based ink with an activator that destroys the garment's dye during curing and can leave pigment in its place. Very soft print on dark cotton with no white base.
techniques.garment_colour: dark or medium, dyed with dischargeable reactive dyes

cotton_percent_min.note: Most suppliers say 100% cotton only and that blends will not discharge. One guide accepts blends with at least 80% cotton. Treat blends as 'test first'.

activator_percent_by_weight.note: Ranges seen: 3-5, 3-6, 3-8 and 5-10. Use the ink maker's figure.

pot_life_hours.note: Sources give 4-8, 8 and 12 hours after adding activator.

cure_temp_c.published: 320 F; one trade guide gives 149-177 C

cure_time_s.note: Minimum 90 s; a trade guide recommends a full 2-3 minutes with good air flow.

risks: Result depends on the fabric dye; always test the actual fabric lot
Final shade is ink pigment plus the discharged ground colour
Activator (zinc formaldehyde sulfoxylate type) releases formaldehyde on curing: ventilation and buyer chemical restrictions must be checked

techniques.name: Non-PVC print
techniques.what_it_is: Plastisol-like result using water-based, silicone or hybrid inks without PVC or phthalates. Softer feel.
risks: Parameters depend fully on the ink brand

techniques.name: Silicone print
techniques.what_it_is: Silicone ink with good wash durability, soft hand and high stretch.
risks: No process parameters were verified in this research; take catalyst %, mesh and cure from the ink maker

techniques.name: Puff (emboss) print
techniques.what_it_is: Plastisol with a heat-activated foaming additive that expands on curing to give a raised, soft 3D surface.

mesh_tpi.note: Above 110 starves the deposit. One supplier allows 40-110.

cure_temp_c.note: Standard puff plastisol 143-166 C (290-330 F). Low-cure puff additives cure at 127-132 C (260-270 F) and must not be overheated.

risks: Not for fine detail
Poor air permeability, so avoid large areas
The raised effect can flatten after repeated washing
Height depends on ink deposit and exact cure temperature
techniques.source: https://www.fn.ink/products/fn-ink%E2%84%A2-puff-ink ; https://thrivescreenprinting.com/what-is-puff-print ; https://pulsemerch.com/puff-screen-printing/ ; user article 'How to Print on Fabric and Textile'

techniques.name: High-density (HD) print
techniques.what_it_is: Very thick ink printed through a thick stencil to give a raised print with sharp edges and a flat top. It does not expand like puff.

mesh_tpi.note: 24T-43T. Finer raised detail may use up to 160-200.

stencil_thickness_micron.note: Capillary film of 200-400 micron is commonly recommended.

cure_temp_c.note: The whole thick film must reach 160 C (320 F); slow the belt. Some products cure at 163-193 C (325-380 F).

risks: Cracking if the thick film is under-cured or the fabric stretches a lot
Long cure time
Best for letters, numbers, borders and geometric shapes
techniques.source: https://lancergroup.com/wp-content/uploads/834835-HD1.pdf ; https://anatol.com/blog/5-tips-for-creating-eye-popping-screen-prints-with-high-density-ink ; user article 'How to Print on Fabric and Textile'

techniques.name: Suede ink print
techniques.what_it_is: Additive mixed into plastisol to give a suede-like feel.

techniques.name: Glitter print
techniques.what_it_is: Large reflective flakes carried in a clear base for a sparkle effect.

mesh_tpi.note: Flakes must pass the mesh. Finer 'sparkle' grades run 60-86. One general guide says 86-110, which is too fine for coarse glitter.

risks: Fine detail is not possible at these mesh counts
Usually printed last, or just before a flash

techniques.name: Metallic / shimmer print
techniques.what_it_is: Small metallic particles in the ink. Smoother and subtler than glitter.

mesh_tpi.note: Shimmer 86-125; metallic 86-110, and very fine-particle metallics up to 156-230.

risks: Check particle size with the ink maker before choosing mesh

techniques.name: Foil print
techniques.what_it_is: An adhesive (or plastisol) is screen printed and cured, then a metallic foil sheet is heat-pressed on. The foil stays only where the adhesive is.

adhesive_mesh_tpi.note: 24T-43T, thick even deposit. Too much adhesive loses fine detail.

adhesive_cure_temp_c.note: 320 F for the named foil adhesives; one foil brand says 140-150 C for 3 min. Follow the adhesive maker.

press_temp_c.note: Foil suppliers say stay under 160 C (320 F) because excess heat damages colour and release. Press-maker guides quote 166-191 C (330-375 F).

peel.value: cold (most common); some foils allow warm peel

risks: Over-heating or re-pressing tarnishes the foil
Uneven pressure gives patchy foil
Wash durability must be tested

techniques.name: Flock print
techniques.what_it_is: Adhesive is printed, then short fibres (rayon, nylon, polyester, cotton) are applied, usually electrostatically, to give a velvet-like surface. Can also be applied as a ready-made flock transfer.

adhesive_cure_temp_c.note: 275-325 F through the whole adhesive layer (plastisol adhesive). The flock insulates, so more heat or a slower belt is needed.

transfer_press_temp_c.note: 300-350 F for 5-60 s, from a patent example only.

adhesive_mesh_tpi.note: Not verified. A thick adhesive layer is required.

risks: Under-cured adhesive: test by scratching
Messy process; slow
Multi-colour flock needs one adhesive pass per colour or a flock transfer

techniques.name: Caviar bead print
techniques.what_it_is: Glue is printed in the design shape and small resin beads are applied to it.
risks: Bead loss in wash; check child-safety rules for small parts on kidswear

techniques.name: Distressed / khadi print
techniques.what_it_is: A worn, cracked or vintage look. This is mainly an artwork treatment (texture knocked out of the design) printed with a normal ink system.

techniques.name: Sticker / plastisol transfer print
techniques.what_it_is: The design is printed on release paper first and fused to the garment with heat and pressure.
risks: Press settings come from the transfer maker

techniques.name: Spot colour screen print
techniques.what_it_is: One screen per solid colour. Best for logos, text and flat graphics.
techniques.screens: number of colours, plus white base on dark garments
techniques.dark_garment_note: On a dark garment, a white print colour can also serve as the base for colours printed over it, so it does not always need a separate base screen.

techniques.name: Spot colour with halftone gradient
techniques.what_it_is: A spot ink that fades out through halftone dots, either into the garment or over another ink (for example blue fading over a white logo). One screen per ink.
techniques.screens: one per ink; the ink underneath may also serve as the base

mesh_tpi.note: For the fading ink. Mesh should be 4 to 5 times the halftone LPI; garment work is typically 45 to 55 LPI.

solid_ink_mesh_tpi.note: For the solid ink underneath; a white on a dark garment uses the lower end.

risks: Dot gain shortens or darkens the fade
Fine dots at the end of the fade can drop out on coarse mesh
Registration between the two screens shows at the edge of the shape
techniques.floor_note: Example confirmed by Ravi on 15 Nov 2026: white solid logo with blue halftone over it on a black T-shirt, 2 screens, or 3 with a separate flashed base.

techniques.name: CMYK four-colour process screen print
techniques.what_it_is: Cyan, magenta, yellow and black halftone screens whose transparent inks overlap to build full-colour images.

mesh_tpi.note: For process colour on light shirts. Mesh should be 4-5 times the halftone LPI.

risks: Not for dark garments without a white base, where simulated process is normally used
Dot gain and registration shift colours across a bulk run
Exact brand colours are safer as separate spot inks

techniques.name: Simulated process screen print
techniques.what_it_is: Photo-like artwork built from halftones of several opaque spot inks, normally over a white base on dark garments, with a highlight white last.
techniques.screens: base white + chosen spot inks (often 4-8) + highlight white

techniques.name: DTG (direct-to-garment) digital print
techniques.what_it_is: Inkjet printing of CMYK inks (plus white on dark garments) straight onto the finished garment. No screens.
suitable_fibres: cotton_polyester_blend (one ink maker: up to 50% polyester)

pretreatment.value: required on dark garments so the white ink sits on the surface

cure_time_s.note: About 90 s is commonly quoted; dark garments with white ink take longer than light ones.

techniques.best_for: Small quantities, many colours, photo artwork, personalisation
risks: Limited print area
Extra cost and steps on coloured garments
Slower per piece than screen printing for bulk
techniques.source: https://www.dupont.com/content/dam/dupont/amer/us/en/artistri/public/documents/en/DI-NA0031-EN-PDS_DTG_pigment_inks.pdf ; https://jotoimagingsupplies.com/blogs/blogs/how-to-apply-pretreatment-fluid-to-garments-a-complete-step-by-step-guide ; user article 'How to Print on Fabric and Textile'

techniques.name: DTF (direct-to-film) transfer
techniques.what_it_is: CMYK plus a white backing is printed on PET film, coated with adhesive powder, cured, then heat-pressed onto the garment.

press_temp_c.note: Lower (about 138-150 C) is advised on polyester.

risks: Film-like feel that sits on the fabric
Not in the user's articles; added from web research

techniques.name: Dye sublimation print
techniques.what_it_is: Disperse dye is printed on paper and turned to gas by heat so it enters polyester fibre. No hand feel, very durable.
techniques.garment_colour: white or light only (there is no white ink)

polyester_percent_min.note: Not verified. Colour gets weaker as polyester content falls.

techniques.source: https://dtfdatabase.com/blog/heat-pressing-polyester-htv-dtf-temperature-iron-burn-repair-guide/ ; https://dtftransfers.com/blogs/news/dtf-dark-garments ; user article 'How to Print on Fabric and Textile'

techniques.name: Digital print with reactive dyes
techniques.what_it_is: Inkjet printing on fabric with reactive dyes. Bright, durable colour; suits cellulosics such as viscose. Needs steaming and washing.
risks: More complex and costly than pigment digital printing; more water use
techniques.source: User article 'How to Print on Fabric and Textile'

techniques.name: Digital print with pigment inks
techniques.what_it_is: Inkjet printing on prepared fabric with pigment inks, fixed by heat. Faster and cheaper than reactive; less bright, lower wet rub fastness.
techniques.source: User article 'How to Print on Fabric and Textile'

techniques.name: All-over print (AOP): rotary or flat-bed screen
techniques.what_it_is: A repeating design printed on fabric before cutting. Rotary screens suit long continuous runs; one screen per colour.
nira_checks: Thinnest line in the design against the minimum printable line
techniques.source: User article 'How to Print on Fabric and Textile'

techniques.name: Burn-out (devoré) print
techniques.what_it_is: An acid-forming paste is printed on a blended fabric and heated. The cellulose fibre is destroyed in the printed area and washed out, leaving a sheer pattern of the other fibre.

burnout_agent.value: sodium hydrogen sulphate (sodium bisulfate) or aluminium sulphate

heat_step.note: A craft source gives 170 C for 5 min. Factory conditions not verified.

cost_usd_per_kg_print.note: Example in the article; out of date as a price.

risks: High process loss must be added to fabric consumption and cost
Over-heating can damage the remaining polyester
High sampling cost

techniques.name: Disperse dye print on polyester (direct style)
techniques.what_it_is: Screen printing polyester with disperse dye paste, then fixing the dye into the fibre with steam or dry heat, followed by reduction clearing.

fixation_methods.note: Carrier needed; allows dyes of low sublimation fastness
Continuous; 10-15% colour yield lost; needs dyes of high sublimation fastness

techniques.after_treatment: Reduction clearing at 60 C for 20 min with 2 g/l caustic soda and 2 g/l sodium hydrosulphite, then wash
techniques.source: User article on print fixation methods for polyester

techniques.name: Disperse-reactive print on polyester/cotton
techniques.what_it_is: A paste containing disperse dye (for the polyester) and reactive dye (for the cotton), so both fibres take colour evenly.

rules.dye_split_by_blend: disperse dye share = polyester %, reactive dye share = cotton %. Example: 70/30 blend at 3 g dye per 100 g paste gives 2.1 g disperse and 0.9 g reactive.
rules.fixation: Dry at 80 C, then pressure steam at 125-130 C, 1-2 bar, 25-30 min
rules.after_treatment: Cold rinse, hot wash, soap at the boil with 2-3 g/l non-ionic detergent, rinse

techniques.source: User article 'Printing of P/C Blended Fabric Using Disperse-Reactive System'

non_print_decorations.note: Tech packs often mix prints with other decorations. NIRA records these and passes them through, but does not engineer them.

tech_pack_term_map.note: Words commonly seen on buyer tech packs, mapped to technique ids in this file.

change_log: v2 (15 Nov 2026): added spot_halftone_gradient, garment_colour_principles and floor notes after a device test on a real garment photo.

rules: Measure the garment colour from the image. Do not assume pure black or pure white.
On a dark or coloured garment, areas that match the garment carry no ink: the fabric shows through.
Never plan a screen in the garment colour.
White base goes only under the print, with a choke. A white print colour can also act as the base for colours printed over it.
Count screens from real print colours and their families, not from every shade a photo contains.
garment_colour_principles.floor_confirmation: Confirmed by Ravi on 15 Nov 2026 for a white + blue gradient logo on a black T-shirt.
